title: Kingdom of Pergamon
capsule: The Attalid Kingdom of Pergamon was a Hellenistic state in western Asia Minor founded when Philetaerus broke from Seleucid control around 281 BCE, becoming fully independent under Attalus I (r. 241–197 BCE), who repelled the Galatian raids and styled himself king. Under Eumenes II (r. 197–159 BCE) Pergamon reached its greatest extent, receiving vast Seleucid and Macedonian territory after allying with Rome; the city became a major cultural center, famed for its library and the Altar of Zeus. The last king, Attalus III, died without a legitimate heir in 133 BCE and bequeathed his kingdom to Rome, which organized it as the province of Asia by 126 BCE, ending the dynasty.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The Attalid kingdom's territory is documented through Roman administrative records and archaeological evidence from Pergamon; boundaries shifted significantly with each war and treaty but are reasonably well attested.
